newsitem.title: UK: Analysts sceptical about G3 yen-intervention talk.
newsitem.headline: Analysts sceptical about G3 yen-intervention talk.

text.p: Sudden rumours about the possibility of internationally-coordinated intervention to cap the dollar/yen exchange rate were dismissed by analysts on Wednesday as speculation and conjecture.
Traders said background rumblings about an imminent move by the U.S., German and Japanese central banks to prevent further weakening of the Japanese currency have weighed on the dollar this week.

Speculation increased on Wednesday when the Japanese news agency Kyodo, citing a senior international monetary source, reported that the so-called Group of Three (G3) nations were exploring the possibility of joint intervention to sell dollars for yen.
"It's very hard to believe that even if they did want to intervene, they would flag it in advance so publicly," said Jeremy Stretch, foreign exchange strategist at NatWest Markets.
Market chatter was fuelled when a Japanese Ministry of Finance official said Japan could use its $220 billion worth of reserves in the foreign exchange market promptly if needed.

Yet currency analysts said most official comment on intervention is coming only from Japan. If there was a move to intervene on the dollar/yen rate, there was little likelihood of a coordinated international effort right now.

The Bank of Japan and U.S. Federal Reserve last intervened together to cap dollar/yen in January 1992 when the rate stood just below 130 yen. Analysts said the signal sent to the market then was partly responsible for the dollar/yen's fall to record lows in the years that followed.

A Bundesbank spokeswoman declined to comment on the Kyodo report, saying Germany stood by the G7 statement in Washington late last month. The G7 said exchange rates should reflect fundamentals and excess volatility was undesirable.
"The idea of some new G3 agreement seems a bit ridiculous," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS in London.

"There are long-standing arrangements in place about this sort of international coordination and, in any event, it really is just up to Japan at the moment," he said. "It's not as if they don't have the ammunition themselves."
Japanese external reserves totalled $219.992 billion in April, well over twice the reserves of either the U.S. or Germany.

Traders also pointed to comments from Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of MOF's International Finance division, about the funding of intervention. He said the process of selling Treasury bills to provide dollar liquidity for intervention was self-defeating as it often advertised central bank intentions to the market in advance.
Analysts said Sakibara's desire to keep the machinations of intervention covert further illustrated why such a high-profile story on G3 intervention talks was unlikely to be accurate.
Analysts said comments from the U.S. and Germany may show uneasiness with further dollar gains but they display no desire to see the dollar go into reverse.

Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said on Tuesday that the German central bank could not welcome further dollar gains. But a spokesman stressed later that Welteke was happy with the dollar about current levels.

"It's very odd for the market to get so worried right now -- the dollar is rangebound at levels which are not particularly exciting," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
